problem: Source says Major H. 'related the following fact'; candidate says 'told me the following story', which casts doubt on a report Tocqueville presents as fact.
replacement: a [ The native of North America holds on to his opinions and even the most insignificant of his habits with a tenacity that has no parallel in history. For more than two hundred years the wandering tribes of North America have been in daily contact with the whites, and they have never taken from them either a custom or an idea. Yet the Europeans have had a powerful influence over the savages: they have made them more licentious, but not more European. In the summer of 1831 I happened to be beyond Lake Michigan, at a place called Green Bay, which serves as the farthest frontier between the United States and the Native Americans on the northwestern side. There I met an American officer, Major H., who talked to me at length about the inflexibility of the Native American character and then related the following fact: “I formerly knew a young Indian,” he said, “who had been educated at a college in New England, where he had greatly distinguished himself, and had acquired the external appearance of a member of civilized society. When the war broke out between ourselves and the English in 1810, I saw this young man again; he was serving in our army, at the head of the warriors of his tribe, for the Indians were admitted among the ranks of the Americans, upon condition that they would abstain from their horrible custom of scalping their victims. On the evening of the battle of . . ., C. came and sat himself down by the fire of our bivouac. I asked him what had been his fortune that day: he related his exploits; and growing warm and animated by the recollection of them, he concluded by suddenly opening the breast of his coat, saying, ‘You must not betray me—see here!’ And I actually beheld,” said the Major, “between his body and his shirt, the skin and hair of an English head, still dripping with gore.”]

problem: 'received William Penn' became 'welcomed', adding a warmth the source does not state.
replacement: None of the Native American tribes that once lived in the territory of New England — the Naragansetts, the Mohicans, the Pecots — exists any longer except in human memory. The Lenapes, who received William Penn on the banks of the Delaware a hundred and fifty years ago, have disappeared; and I myself met the last of the Iroquois, who were begging for alms. The nations I have named once covered the country all the way to the seacoast, but today a traveler must go more than a hundred leagues into the interior of the continent to find a Native American. These wild tribes have not only withdrawn; they have been destroyed. *b And as they give way or perish, an immense and growing people takes their place. There is no recorded instance of such prodigious growth or such rapid destruction, and it is not hard to describe how the destruction takes place.

problem: 'ejectment' (forcible legal eviction) softened to 'removal'; the point of the sentence is the legal form of an ejection.
replacement: The ejection of the Native Americans very often takes place today in a regular and, so to speak, legal manner. When the European population begins to approach the edge of the wilderness inhabited by a savage tribe, the government of the United States usually sends envoys to them. The envoys gather the Native Americans on a large plain, eat and drink with them first, and then address them in the following way: “What have you to do in the land of your fathers? Before long, you must dig up their bones in order to live. In what respect is the country you inhabit better than another? Are there no woods, marshes, or prairies, except where you dwell? And can you live nowhere but under your own sun? Beyond those mountains which you see at the horizon, beyond the lake which bounds your territory on the west, there lie vast countries where beasts of chase are found in great abundance; sell your lands to us, and go to live happily in those solitudes.” After saying this, they lay out before the eyes of the Native Americans firearms, woolen garments, kegs of brandy, glass necklaces, tinsel bracelets, earrings, and mirrors. *g If, after seeing all these riches, the Native Americans still hesitate, it is hinted that they have no means of refusing the consent that is demanded, and that the government itself will soon be unable to protect their rights. What are they to do? Half convinced and half forced, they go to live in new deserts, where the importunate whites will not let them stay in peace for ten years. This is how the Americans obtain, at a very low price, whole provinces that the richest sovereigns of Europe could not buy. *h
